podcast.title: Billboard Magazine Origin
podcast.body: The name "Country and Western" was coined by Billboard magazine, initially not as a descriptor for a single genre but as a title for a collection of different genres on their charts. It combined "Country music" from the Eastern US and "Western music" from the West. "Country and Western... were names that were coined by Billboard magazine."

podcast.title: Conservative Nature of Top-Tier Shows
podcast.body: Higher-tier country shows like the Grand Ole Opry, while popular, were extraordinarily conservative, adhering to strict formulas and limiting experimentation. "Girls like the Upree, while the popular, were also extraordinarily conservative."

podcast.title: Crossover with R&B for Male Jump Band Artists
podcast.body: Generally, the few country musicians who played R&B songs primarily covered music originally recorded by male jump band artists like Louis Jordan or Big Joe Turner, rather than female R&B artists whose music was closer to jazz. "Generally, the few who did that were performing music originally recorded by male jump band artists like Louis Jordan or Big Joe Turner."

podcast.title: Dominance of Live Variety Radio Shows (1950s)
podcast.body: In the 1950s, country and western music was primarily dominated by live variety shows broadcast by different radio stations, which formed a distinct hierarchy with the Grand Ole Opry at the top. "the dominant force in country and western music was a series of live variety shows that would be broadcast by different radio stations."

podcast.title: Early Target Market for Fender
podcast.body: Leo Fender initially targeted country and western musicians, particularly those who were already using lap steel guitars, as the primary audience for his solid-body Spanish-style guitars. "Leo's first target were the country and western musicians who were into lap steel guitars."

podcast.title: Experimental Nature of Lower-Tier Shows
podcast.body: Lower-rung hillbilly shows, such as the Old Dominion Barn Dance, were more experimental and allowed for greater deviation from the straight formula insisted upon by the top shows, providing a space for artists like Janice Martin to try different styles. "the further down the rungs you got, the more experimental the hillbilly shows could be."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Hierarchy of Live Shows
podcast.body: There was a clear hierarchy among country and western live variety shows, with the Grand Ole Opry at the pinnacle, followed by the Louisiana Hayride, and then shows like the Old Dominion Barn Dance. This hierarchy dictated an artist's status and audience reach. "At the very top of the chain was the grand ol' Opry."
